cpu_bound.independent: Process pool over independent iterations: multiprocessing.Pool(...).map / ProcessPoolExecutor.map (threads do not help CPU-bound Python: GIL). Large data: chunked processing with Pool.map(fn, items, chunksize=...) or explicit chunks.
cpu_bound.mergeable_reduction: Map-reduce with a process pool: each worker processes a chunk and returns a small partial (Counter, per-chunk lists); the parent merges partials in one linear pass.
cpu_bound.true_shared_state: Process pool with multiprocessing.Manager or multiprocessing.shared_memory for the shared structure; minimise synchronised writes (prefer per-worker partials merged at the end).
cpu_bound.loop_carried: Iteration N depends on N-1: keep the dependent chain sequential; parallelize only independent sub-work inside each iteration, or restructure the algorithm (prefix/scan, batching) first.

io_bound.independent: Many independent requests: asyncio + aiohttp/aiofiles when available; with legacy blocking libraries use ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N); mixed sync/async code: asyncio.to_thread(); databases: connection pooling + async drivers.
io_bound.mergeable_reduction: ThreadPoolExecutor or asyncio.gather over the I/O calls, then merge results in the parent.
io_bound.true_shared_state: Threads with a lock around the shared structure (or an asyncio.Lock); keep critical sections tiny.
io_bound.loop_carried: Sequential dependency between requests: pipeline/prefetch the next request while processing the current one; otherwise keep sequential.

data_parallel.independent: Vectorize first: NumPy array ops / pandas built-in vectorized methods instead of Python loops; then numba (@jit(nopython=True, parallel=True) with prange) or dask for out-of-core; GPU only if available (CuPy/JAX).
data_parallel.mergeable_reduction: Vectorized per-chunk reductions (np.add.reduce, groupby-agg) combined at the end; dask for data larger than memory.
data_parallel.true_shared_state: NumPy array in multiprocessing.shared_memory; workers attach by name and work on disjoint slices.
data_parallel.loop_carried: Use cumulative ufuncs (np.cumsum, ufunc.accumulate) or numba for the sequential recurrence.

mixed.independent: Hybrid pipeline: CPU-heavy parts in a ProcessPoolExecutor via loop.run_in_executor, I/O parts with asyncio.gather (or a thread pool).
mixed.mergeable_reduction: Hybrid pipeline (process pool for CPU, async/threads for I/O) with a final merge in the parent.
mixed.true_shared_state: Separate the CPU and I/O stages with queues (producer-consumer); keep the shared state in one owner process.
mixed.loop_carried: Overlap I/O of step N+1 with CPU of step N (producer-consumer queue); the dependent chain stays sequential.

no_numeric_libs_fallback: NumPy/pandas/numba are not importable here: do not vectorize with them; use a process pool over pure-Python chunks (stdlib multiprocessing) instead.

balancing.uniform: Static partitioning: equal chunks (np.array_split or items[i*n//W:(i+1)*n//W]); streaming input -> round-robin items[i::W]; large items -> size-aware partitioning.
balancing.variable_predictable: Weighted distribution: sort items by estimated cost descending and assign each to the least-loaded worker (LPT / greedy bin packing); weight = a cheap cost proxy such as text length or row count.
balancing.variable_unpredictable: Dynamic scheduling: many small tasks pulled by idle workers (Pool.imap/map with a modest chunksize, or submit + wait(FIRST_COMPLETED) refill loop).
balancing.long_tail: Work stealing / dynamic scheduling with the largest items submitted first, plus time limits; split giant items into subtasks so no single task dominates.

resource_constraints.memory_bound_workers: Memory-aware assignment: cap concurrent big items per worker; pass ids/slices, not whole objects.
resource_constraints.network_costs: Locality-aware placement: send work to where the data already is.

shared_input.fork: Large read-only input (index, model, corpus): set it as a module-level global BEFORE creating a fork-context pool (multiprocessing.get_context('fork')); children inherit it copy-on-write with zero pickling. Never send it with every task.
shared_input.no_fork: No fork start method: pass the large read-only input once per worker via Pool(initializer=..., initargs=(data,)) and store it in a module global; for NumPy arrays use multiprocessing.shared_memory.

always: Send workers only what they need (e.g. (id, text) tuples, not full objects) and return compact results; pickling both ways is the main parallel overhead.
Process in chunks and discard: do not build every intermediate for the whole dataset when a streaming pass works.
Measure: tracemalloc (snapshot.statistics('lineno')) or resource.getrusage(...).ru_maxrss for peak RSS; sys.getsizeof is shallow only.
memory_goal: Large collections of small objects: __slots__ / dataclass(slots=True) / namedtuple (roughly 40-60% less per instance).
Lists built all at once: generators (yield / yield from) and process-and-discard.
Repeated strings: sys.intern or pandas category dtype.
Numeric data in lists: NumPy arrays (8 bytes/float64); DataFrames: downcast dtypes (pd.to_numeric(downcast=...)) and sparse arrays for mostly-empty data - only when NumPy/pandas are importable.
Whole-file loads: chunked reading or mmap / np.memmap.
Intermediate copies: in-place operations and views instead of copies.

Objects never freed / unbounded caches / global accumulation / large temporaries: break circular refs with weakref, lru_cache(maxsize=...), bounded deque or periodic clear, context managers for explicit cleanup, del + gc.collect() for big temporaries; closures should capture only needed values; unregister event listeners.

exactness: Reuse the baseline's own helper functions (import them) for tokenizing/parsing/per-item math so per-item results are identical.
Floating-point sums depend on order: accumulate in the same order as the baseline (same dict/insertion order); adding 0.0 terms the baseline adds is harmless (x + 0.0 == x).
Stable sorts keep insertion order for ties: build lists in the baseline's item order, or sort by (-score, original_position) after merging out-of-order chunks.
Reassemble parallel results in input order (map, or index by position) - never in completion order (as_completed) when order matters.
Keep the baseline's return types and container types (dict vs set vs list, dataclass fields) so equality checks pass.
pitfalls: GIL trap: threads do not speed up CPU-bound Python; use processes.
Pickle failures: lambdas, nested functions and nested classes cannot be sent to process pools; use module-level functions.
Memory explosion: every process gets its own copy of pickled data; share big read-only data via fork/initializer/shared memory.
Async in sync: adding async to one function is not enough; the whole call chain must be restructured.
Over-parallelization: pool start-up and pickling exceed the gains for small workloads (< ~1000 cheap items); keep a sequential fast path below a size threshold.
Fix the algorithm first: an O(n*m) loop parallelized over W workers is still O(n*m)/W; a linear rewrite usually beats it.
Amdahl: the serial part (merge, final sort) bounds speedup at 1/((1-p)+p/W); measure it and keep the parent's merge linear.
Worker count above usable CPUs (cgroup quota, affinity) adds contention, not speed; bound workers explicitly.
Python 3.14+ and macOS default to spawn/forkserver: module globals are not inherited; use an explicit fork context or an initializer, and guard script entry with if __name__ == '__main__'.
Over-partitioning: too many tiny tasks cost more in IPC than they save; batch small items (aim for ~2-8 chunks per worker).
Starvation/stragglers: one huge task at the end of the queue leaves workers idle; submit largest first or split it.
verification_checklist: Output matches the sequential version for test inputs (exactly, or within the tolerance the task states).
No race conditions: shared mutable state is absent or properly synchronized.
Exceptions in workers are caught/propagated (executor.submit for per-item error handling; return_exceptions=True for asyncio.gather).
Resources cleaned up: pools/executors used as context managers, connections released, shared memory closed and unlinked.
Worker count is bounded (default or explicit limit) and the API accepts the worker count the task specifies.
Required imports added; the module imports cleanly in a fresh interpreter.
Work distribution roughly even (load imbalance max/avg < 1.2; measure completion times).
No starvation: all workers stay busy (utilization > 90%).
Stragglers handled (max/median task time < 2.0; timeout/retry or largest-first scheduling).
Results are complete and correct (no items dropped or duplicated across chunks).
Overhead acceptable: parallel version is faster than sequential at the task's worker counts and data sizes (and not slower at 1 worker).
Memory usage measured (reduced, when memory is a goal); no new memory leaks; peak within the container's limit; performance acceptable (generators may add iteration overhead).
